title: Nessus Scan Policies & Vulnerability Scanning
description: Let’s use your scanner to check two practice servers, understand what it finds, make a supported fix and check again. You’ll learn the settings as we use them.
baseline: Nessus 10.12.5 · one scanner, one AlmaLinux 9 target and one Windows Server 2022 target
prerequisite: Your scanner is ready—now let’s give it two practice computers to inspect. We’ll start with a small scan, learn how to read the results, and check a fix together. Here’s the setup we’ll use.

lessons.title: Prepare Your First Scan
lessons.description: Let’s identify our three computers before we touch the scan button.
lessons.what: We’ll make a simple plan that names the scanner and the two computers it may inspect. This helps us keep every later click pointed at the right place.
lessons.why: An address is like a house number. A small typing mistake can send a scan to a computer that was never part of the class.
bestPractices: Keep the Nessus control page on your private lab network.
Count only the two targets you have permission to use, and check that your actual license covers them.
commonMistakes: Port 8834 opens the Nessus management page. It is not the port for every test Nessus runs against a target.
An empty results page may mean no scan ran or some checks failed. It does not prove the targets are safe.

troubleshooting.problem: Nessus is still preparing plugins
troubleshooting.fix: Give it time to finish. If progress seems stuck, look at the service, free disk space and update status before trying a restart.

lessons.pass: You can point to the scanner and both separate targets and explain what you have permission to check.
lessons.exercise: Show your instructor a three-row plan: scanner, AlmaLinux target and Windows target. Explain which two addresses are allowed, keeping private values out of public copies.

quiz.question: Which machines belong in this lab’s target list?
options: Only the two authorized target IPs
quiz.explanation: A short allowlist keeps the scan within the agreed scope.

quiz.question: Does a Nessus install automatically include every template?
quiz.explanation: Check what your real license enables before planning a feature-dependent task.

steps.title: Name three separate machines
steps.where: Private lab notes · no scan launched
actions: Let’s draw three rows in your private notes. Label them Scanner, AlmaLinux target and Windows target. Add each computer’s name and real private IP address.
Look at each machine’s own console and compare its current address with your note. Keep the scanner out of the vulnerability target list; Tenable does not support that kind of self-scan.
Write down who owns the two targets, when you may scan, which checks are allowed, who to contact, and how you would recover. Only the two agreed target IPs go into our scans.
steps.expected: Your notes clearly name the scanner and two separate targets, with the permitted scan boundary.

screenshot.title: Name three separate machines
screenshot.instructions: When you reach this point in your own lab, take a screenshot showing name three separate machines. Keep the relevant controls and computer context visible so you can explain the check. Hide credentials, activation details and private information first. This is your capture checklist; a genuine screenshot is still needed here.

steps.title: Check readiness and license
steps.where: Your workstation browser · verified Nessus HTTPS console
actions: Open your scanner’s verified https://hostname:8834 page and sign in. Go to Settings → About → Overview so we can see which product is actually running.
Write down the version, product edition and plugin-set date, but hide the activation code. Wait for plugin preparation to finish before creating or launching a job.

Read the current target limit and features for your actual license. The 10.12 guide describes Essentials as five IPs with a delayed plugin feed, so an old tutorial’s limits may no longer match your copy.
steps.expected: You can identify the actual product and plugin readiness before creating a job.

screenshot.title: Check readiness and license
screenshot.instructions: When you reach this point in your own lab, take a screenshot showing check readiness and license. Keep the relevant controls and computer context visible so you can explain the check. Hide credentials, activation details and private information first. This is your capture checklist; a genuine screenshot is still needed here.

needs: Finish a Nessus installation class first. Start your separate scanner and two practice targets, and keep their private address list handy.

lessons.title: Check Accounts and Plugin Updates
lessons.description: Check who can control the scanner and how its checks stay up to date.
lessons.what: Let’s review your Nessus login and plugin updates. Your login controls access to the tool; plugins are the individual checks the tool uses.
lessons.why: Fresh checks can recognize newer problems. A clear account and update plan also helps us avoid unexpected access or software-version changes.
bestPractices: Use the account and update time agreed for your lab.
Write down the plugin date with your first scan so you know which check set produced the result.
commonMistakes: An update-plan change may also change the application version. Read the choice before saving it.
The private license file and a plugin archive do different jobs. Don’t upload one in place of the other.

troubleshooting.problem: I cannot find Software Update
troubleshooting.fix: Check your role and product edition. If another Tenable platform manages this scanner, it may control updates instead.

lessons.pass: Your notes name the scanner-account owner, update method and current plugin date without including any password.
lessons.exercise: Write two short update paths in your notes: what your online scanner uses, and what an offline scanner would need. Record the plugin date you actually see.

quiz.question: What are plugins?
quiz.explanation: Plugins tell Nessus what to check and how to report it.

quiz.question: What changed for manual plugin updates in 10.12.5?
options: A matching Tenable signature file is required
quiz.explanation: Use trusted, matching archive and signature files; never bypass signature checks.

steps.title: Review the administrator account
steps.where: Your workstation browser · verified Nessus HTTPS console
actions: Open Settings → Accounts → My Account. Let’s check the account you use to control Nessus. Give it a unique password and keep that password in the approved password manager.

Enter scanner passwords only in the real protected Nessus console, never in SONIC-Academy. If you have Nessus Manager and see Users, review its named accounts and roles there; standalone editions do not use that same multi-user workflow.
Write down who looks after scanner access and account recovery. Give each permitted learner an appropriate account rather than passing around one administrator password.
steps.expected: You know which account controls the scanner and who handles access recovery.

screenshot.title: Review the administrator account
screenshot.instructions: When you reach this point in your own lab, take a screenshot showing review the administrator account. Keep the relevant controls and computer context visible so you can explain the check. Hide credentials, activation details and private information first. This is your capture checklist; a genuine screenshot is still needed here.

steps.title: Inspect the update plan
steps.where: Your workstation browser · verified Nessus HTTPS console
actions: Open Settings → About → Software Update. Read the current application and plugin update choices before changing either one.
For an online standalone scanner, get agreement before updating. If your page offers it, choose Manual Software Update → Update plugins → Continue. Let the update and plugin preparation finish.

An offline or centrally managed scanner uses its own update process. With version 10.12.5, a manual plugin import needs its matching Tenable signature. A tar.gz filename alone does not tell us that the file is the correct plugin bundle.
steps.expected: You can explain how your scanner updates its software and plugins, including any offline limitation.

screenshot.title: Inspect the update plan
screenshot.instructions: When you reach this point in your own lab, take a screenshot showing inspect the update plan. Keep the relevant controls and computer context visible so you can explain the check. Hide credentials, activation details and private information first. This is your capture checklist; a genuine screenshot is still needed here.

needs: Sign in to the real Nessus console. Have your product name and online or offline update plan ready.

lessons.title: Understand Templates and Policies
lessons.description: Learn the difference between a ready-made scan recipe and one you save yourself.
lessons.what: A template is a recipe Tenable provides. A policy is a recipe you save with the settings you chose. A scan adds the target computers and the time to run.
lessons.why: Knowing these three pieces makes the next pages less confusing. You don’t have to guess what every advanced switch does before making a useful first scan.
bestPractices: Start with Basic Network Scan for the first agreed baseline. A starting point is the result we keep for comparison later.
commonMistakes: Finding a live host is useful, but a discovery result is not a full vulnerability assessment.
Some templates intentionally show fewer settings. Don’t assume every Advanced setting belongs in every template.

troubleshooting.problem: My page is missing a setting
troubleshooting.fix: Check the chosen template, product edition and your role. A picture from another product may show controls you do not have.

lessons.pass: You can explain template, policy and scan in your own words and find their matching pages.
lessons.exercise: Show a classmate a template, the policy list and a scan job. Use the recipe idea to explain how they fit together.

quiz.question: Which template checks whether approved credentials work?
quiz.explanation: Credential Validation is a focused login-checking template when available.

quiz.question: What does a saved policy need before it becomes a specific scan?
options: An authorized target and run settings
quiz.explanation: The scan supplies its targets and schedule; the policy supplies reusable settings.

steps.title: Find the built-in templates
steps.where: Your workstation browser · verified Nessus HTTPS console
actions: Click Scans → New Scan. Take a look for Basic Network Scan, Host Discovery and Credential Validation. Your license may not show all three.

Read the descriptions before choosing. Basic Network Scan checks for vulnerabilities. Host Discovery looks for live systems and ports. Credential Validation checks whether the login you supplied works.
Leave Launch alone for now. Write down any unavailable or locked choices as license differences. This class uses network scans; agent and web-application workflows are separate.
steps.expected: You can explain what each available template is meant to check without launching it.

screenshot.title: Find the built-in templates
screenshot.instructions: When you reach this point in your own lab, take a screenshot showing find the built-in templates. Keep the relevant controls and computer context visible so you can explain the check. Hide credentials, activation details and private information first. This is your capture checklist; a genuine screenshot is still needed here.

steps.title: Find saved policies
steps.where: Your workstation browser · verified Nessus HTTPS console
actions: Return to Scans and click Policies on the left. This is where we look for saved scan recipes, not the actual scan results.
Look at any existing policies without changing them. A policy you save can appear under User Defined when you create a scan.
Try saying the parts aloud: “My lab starting point policy, plus the Alma target address and an agreed time, makes a scan job.”
steps.expected: You have found the policy list and understand how a saved recipe becomes a scan job.

screenshot.title: Find saved policies
screenshot.instructions: When you reach this point in your own lab, take a screenshot showing find saved policies. Keep the relevant controls and computer context visible so you can explain the check. Hide credentials, activation details and private information first. This is your capture checklist; a genuine screenshot is still needed here.

needs: Open the Nessus console with plugins ready. We will check choices here without launching a scan.

lessons.title: Create a Basic Network Scan
lessons.description: Create a first scan job, give it a useful name and save it without running it yet.
lessons.what: We’ll fill in a Basic Network Scan for one target. Think of this as writing an inspection appointment before we actually visit the computer.
lessons.why: Saving first gives us time to check the target, credentials and safe settings. There’s no prize for clicking Launch early.
bestPractices: Give the job a useful name and enter the exact target IP you checked.
Keep this first scan manual so it waits until you are ready.
commonMistakes: Adding /24 can turn one address into a whole subnet. Don’t use it when you have permission for only one host.
Save the job first. We have more checks to finish before Launch.

troubleshooting.problem: The Save button is unavailable
troubleshooting.fix: Look for a missing name or target field. Also check that plugin preparation has finished before trying to create or launch scans.

lessons.pass: The saved scan names one permitted target and has no automatic schedule enabled.
lessons.exercise: Ask a partner to compare the saved target address with the address displayed on your AlmaLinux target’s own console.

quiz.question: What should the first target field contain?
quiz.explanation: Use the address you checked at the practice target’s console.

quiz.question: Why save before launching?
quiz.explanation: Saving gives you a chance to check the job before it sends traffic.

steps.title: Create and name the job
steps.where: Your workstation browser · verified Nessus HTTPS console
actions: Let’s make the first job. Click Scans → New Scan → Basic Network Scan. We’ll save it first and give ourselves time to check it.
Under Settings → Basic → General, give the job a useful name, such as SONIC-Alma-Baseline. In the description, note the owner and why this practice scan exists.
In Targets, type only the Alma target’s checked private IP. Use the address from its console, not a sample address or the Nessus scanner’s address.
steps.expected: The job has a clear name and the one Alma target address you checked.

screenshot.title: Create and name the job
screenshot.instructions: When you reach this point in your own lab, take a screenshot showing create and name the job. Keep the relevant controls and computer context visible so you can explain the check. Hide credentials, activation details and private information first. This is your capture checklist; a genuine screenshot is still needed here.

steps.title: Save without scheduling
steps.where: Your workstation browser · verified Nessus HTTPS console
actions: Open Basic → Schedule. Leave Enable Schedule Off for this first job so it waits for you to launch it deliberately.
Read the target and template back once more. Click Save, not Launch.
Return to My Scans and find the job by name. We’ll add credentials and review safety before we run it.
steps.expected: The job appears in My Scans and waits for a manual launch.

screenshot.title: Save without scheduling
screenshot.instructions: When you reach this point in your own lab, take a screenshot showing save without scheduling. Keep the relevant controls and computer context visible so you can explain the check. Hide credentials, activation details and private information first. This is your capture checklist; a genuine screenshot is still needed here.

needs: Have the AlmaLinux target’s verified private IP ready. We will create a job, then check it before launch.

lessons.title: Build a Custom Scan Policy
lessons.description: Save a set of scan settings so you can reuse and explain it.
lessons.what: Let’s build a custom policy, which is our saved scan recipe. Then we’ll create a job that uses that recipe for the AlmaLinux target.
lessons.why: A named policy makes it easier to repeat a scan and tell someone which settings were used. We’ll still check what your license actually provides.
bestPractices: After a permitted settings change, add a short revision note to the policy description so you can tell versions apart.
commonMistakes: Keep the starting point policy steady while comparing a before-and-after result. If it changes, record the difference.
A scan that uses a linked policy inherits some settings. Edit those in the policy rather than assuming the job can override them.

troubleshooting.problem: User Defined shows nothing
troubleshooting.fix: Check that you saved the policy under the account you are using. Make sure plugin preparation is finished too.

lessons.pass: You can find the saved policy and point to a scan that uses it, or clearly explain the feature your license does not provide.
lessons.exercise: Write a short revision note for the policy: what it is for, who owns it, and which two lab targets are allowed.

quiz.question: Where do saved custom policies appear when making a scan?
quiz.explanation: User Defined contains available saved policies.

quiz.question: Where should inherited Discovery settings be changed?
quiz.explanation: Policy-based scans inherit these controls from the policy.

steps.title: Create the policy
steps.where: Your workstation browser · verified Nessus HTTPS console
actions: Click Scans → Policies → New Policy. Choose Advanced Scan if your edition offers it. If that choice is missing, follow the limited-license branch below rather than trying another product’s instructions.
In Basic settings, call the policy SONIC-Approved-Server-Policy. Add a description explaining that it is for the two agreed targets on this private lab network.

Keep the initial defaults and save. We’ll check discovery, ports, safe checks and plugins next. If your license does not offer custom policies, record that limit and keep using your saved Basic Network Scan.
steps.expected: Your policy is saved, or the missing licensed feature is honestly documented.

screenshot.title: Create the policy
screenshot.instructions: When you reach this point in your own lab, take a screenshot showing create the policy. Keep the relevant controls and computer context visible so you can explain the check. Hide credentials, activation details and private information first. This is your capture checklist; a genuine screenshot is still needed here.

steps.title: Make a job from your policy
steps.where: Your workstation browser · verified Nessus HTTPS console
actions: Now let’s use the saved recipe. Click Scans → New Scan → User Defined and choose SONIC-Approved-Server-Policy.
Call the job SONIC-Policy-Alma and enter the checked Alma target IP. Leave its schedule Off and click Save.
If you need to change inherited Discovery or Advanced settings, go back to the policy. Those are the shared recipe, not independent switches inside this linked job.
steps.expected: You can identify the job that uses the saved policy and where its inherited settings come from.

Keep the relevant controls and computer context visible so you can explain the check. Hide credentials, activation details and private information first. This is your capture checklist; a genuine screenshot is still needed here.

needs: Keep the first saved scan and target list. Check whether your Nessus edition offers custom policies before following that branch.

lessons.title: Set Discovery, Ports, Safe Checks and Exclusions
lessons.description: Choose what the scanner looks at and keep the lab within its agreed limits.
lessons.what: We’ll review host discovery, ports, safe checks, plugin choices and excluded systems. In plain words: which computers can we visit, which doors can we check, and which tests can we use?
lessons.why: A scan can affect the computer it inspects. Careful settings help us learn without accidentally including the router, scanner or another person’s server.
bestPractices: A real company application owner must agree to a production scan. This class practices on the agreed lab targets.
If resources are tight, ask your instructor for a lower allowed concurrency—the number of checks or jobs running at once.
commonMistakes: A slow scan is not a reason to turn off safety checks. Investigate the cause first.
A web-address exclusion does not automatically exclude a computer’s IP address.
A short port list means you checked fewer doors. Don’t call it a full assessment without explaining that limit.

troubleshooting.problem: Nessus says the guest is down
troubleshooting.fix: Check its current console address and the private network route. Review the VMware guest discovery choice before adding more target addresses.

lessons.pass: You can show the safe checks, port coverage, plugin choices and the exact two-target boundary. Unavailable licensed settings remain clearly noted.
lessons.exercise: Point to the exact target field and explain why every other system is outside our scan. Show the safe-checks setting and the port range too.

quiz.question: Do safe checks promise that scanning cannot cause disruption?
options: No; permission and monitoring still matter
quiz.explanation: Safe checks reduce harmful plugin behavior but cannot remove every risk.

quiz.question: Does a web-app URL exclusion exclude an entire network host?
quiz.explanation: Host scope must be controlled by valid network target/rule settings.

steps.title: Review discovery and ports
steps.where: Your workstation browser · verified Nessus HTTPS console
actions: First, choose the route your license supports. If custom policies are unavailable, edit your saved Basic Network Scan and use only its visible settings. Write down any missing control; don’t pretend a locked setting changed.

Open the saved policy’s Settings → Discovery → Host Discovery. For these exact VMware guest targets, follow Tenable’s guidance to set Ping the remote host Off. A guest may not answer the ping method even when we can reach it.
Under Discovery → Port Scanning, check Port Scan Range. Keep the documented default for the broad baseline. Guessing a short list can miss services.

For a separately agreed focused follow-up, a comma list such as 22,80,443,445 is valid. Explain that it covers only those ports. Authenticated local port discovery can also affect what is actually covered.
steps.expected: You can explain which discovery and port choices are in use and what their limits are.

screenshot.title: Review discovery and ports
screenshot.instructions: When you reach this point in your own lab, take a screenshot showing review discovery and ports. Keep the relevant controls and computer context visible so you can explain the check. Hide credentials, activation details and private information first. This is your capture checklist; a genuine screenshot is still needed here.

steps.title: Keep safe checks and review plugins
steps.where: Your workstation browser · verified Nessus HTTPS console
actions: Open Settings → Advanced → General Settings and leave Enable Safe Checks enabled. We’re leaving denial-of-service, brute-force and fragile-device testing out of this beginner lab.

If you are using an Advanced Scan policy, open Plugins and check the enabled families. Keep the normal starting point coverage; don’t enable risky tests or remove checks just to make the results look better.
Save and note the policy revision. Safe checks reduce harmful testing, but they do not promise zero impact. Stop if the target becomes unstable.
steps.expected: Safe checks remain enabled, and you have recorded the actual plugin choices you reviewed.

screenshot.title: Keep safe checks and review plugins
screenshot.instructions: When you reach this point in your own lab, take a screenshot showing keep safe checks and review plugins. Keep the relevant controls and computer context visible so you can explain the check. Hide credentials, activation details and private information first. This is your capture checklist; a genuine screenshot is still needed here.

steps.title: Define and enforce exclusions
steps.where: Your workstation browser · verified Nessus HTTPS console
actions: Write a short “do not scan” list. Include the scanner, physical host, router, domain controllers and every computer outside the two permitted target addresses.
Open each job’s Basic → Targets and remove any address outside our exact two-target list. Using a short positive list is clearer for this lab than guessing exclusion syntax for a broad subnet.

If a company scanner needs a global network exclusion, have its owner use Tenable’s documented reject address/netmask:ports rules through the agreed process. A web-app URL exclusion or a Linux file-search exclusion is a different feature; neither automatically removes a network host from scope.
steps.expected: Only the two intended targets remain in the jobs; every excluded system stays outside that list.

lessons.title: Configure an Authenticated AlmaLinux Scan
lessons.description: Give Nessus a permitted Linux login and check what that login can really inspect.
lessons.what: An outside-only scan looks through the windows. An authenticated scan uses a permitted login to check installed software and settings inside the target.
lessons.why: The inside view can reveal missing updates that a network-only scan misses. Signing in successfully still does not guarantee permission to read every needed item.
bestPractices: When practical, use a dedicated SSH key and protect its private half.
Give the account enough permission for the agreed checks, and clearly record anything it still cannot read.
commonMistakes: The target needs the public key. Keep the matching private key protected on the permitted client or scanner.
A normal user can sign in but may still lack permission to read root-only information.

troubleshooting.problem: The SSH login fails
troubleshooting.fix: Compare the username, SSH port and trusted host identity. Check the source-limited firewall rule and the target’s authentication logs.

troubleshooting.problem: Login works, but some local checks fail
troubleshooting.fix: Read the permission messages and plugin evidence. Agree on only the needed sudo permissions; don’t disable SELinux or grant unrestricted root access to silence the error.

lessons.pass: You can show redacted login-check saved result and explain whether limited permissions left some checks incomplete.
lessons.exercise: Use the actual login and permission results to explain one access gap. If more access is needed, request only the change that the saved result justifies.

quiz.question: Where should scan passwords be entered?
options: In the real protected Nessus credential form
quiz.explanation: This learning platform does not need or store your target secrets.

quiz.question: Does successful SSH login prove every audit ran?
options: No; permissions and plugin evidence matter
quiz.explanation: Authentication and sufficient authorization are separate checks.

steps.title: Prepare the target’s approved account
steps.where: AlmaLinux 9 target console · administrator terminal
actions: Open the separate AlmaLinux target’s console. Run hostname and compare its name and IP with your target list. This check keeps us from creating the scan account on the scanner by mistake.

Use an existing dedicated account that has been permitted for this task. If you need one, have the target owner use the shown commands to create nessusscan. Set the password at its interactive prompt and keep it in the approved password manager.
Check that sshd is active. The target firewall should permit the scanner’s TCP22 connection according to the lab plan. Don’t enable direct root SSH login for this exercise.
steps.command:
hostname
sudo useradd --create-home --shell /bin/bash nessusscan
sudo passwd nessusscan
sudo systemctl status sshd --no-pager

breakdown.meaning: Shows which computer you are administering.
Runs the following administration command with approved elevated rights.
Creates the named local account, its home folder and Bash shell; skip if the approved account already exists.
Asks privately for that account’s password; do not type it into a command or website field here.
Inspects the SSH service without a scrolling pager; this does not start a stopped service.

steps.expected: The target has a dedicated permitted account and a reachable SSH service.

screenshot.title: Prepare the target’s approved account
screenshot.instructions: When you reach this point in your own lab, take a screenshot showing prepare the target’s approved account. Keep the relevant controls and computer context visible so you can explain the check. Hide credentials, activation details and private information first. This is your capture checklist; a genuine screenshot is still needed here.

steps.title: Add SSH credentials to the scan
steps.where: Your workstation browser · verified Nessus HTTPS console
actions: Edit your saved Alma scan or its policy. Open Credentials → Host → SSH; some layouts show SSH directly. This is where we tell Nessus which permitted Linux login to use.

Choose the permitted Password or SSH public key method. Enter the dedicated username and secret only in the real Nessus HTTPS console. For key authentication, give Nessus the protected private key and passphrase; its matching public key belongs on the target.

For checks needing more permission, select the agreed sudo elevation method. Use Attempt Least Privilege when it is available. Have the owner review the required commands with visudo and Tenable’s command-logging process. Don’t copy an unrestricted NOPASSWD: ALL rule just to make errors disappear. Save.
steps.expected: The saved scan has the intended SSH account and agreed privilege method, with secrets kept private.

screenshot.title: Add SSH credentials to the scan
screenshot.instructions: When you reach this point in your own lab, take a screenshot showing add ssh credentials to the scan. Keep the relevant controls and computer context visible so you can explain the check. Hide credentials, activation details and private information first. This is your capture checklist; a genuine screenshot is still needed here.

steps.title: Check credentials before a full scan
steps.where: Your workstation browser · verified Nessus HTTPS console
actions: If your license offers Credential Validation, create a one-target job using the same permitted SSH credentials. Save it and launch it only during the agreed time. If it is unavailable, use the controlled starting point in the launch lesson instead.
When the check finishes, open the host’s informational results and Nessus Scan Information, plugin 19506. Read the credentialed-check status and any local-check or permission messages.
A working login is one checkpoint, not proof that every needed check ran. Read the least-privilege diagnostics and agree on only the permissions the saved result shows are necessary.
steps.expected: Your results show whether login and needed local checks worked, including any permission gap.

Keep the relevant controls and computer context visible so you can explain the check. Hide credentials, activation details and private information first. This is your capture checklist; a genuine screenshot is still needed here.

needs: Use the separate AlmaLinux target, its exact IP and a dedicated permitted scan account. Keep SSH credentials in the real Nessus console, not in class notes.

lessons.title: Configure an Authenticated Windows Scan
lessons.description: Set up a Windows target login without giving the scanner control of the whole domain.
lessons.what: We’ll give Nessus a dedicated account for the Server 2022 target. Windows checks may need to read files, registry settings and management information on that target.
lessons.why: An open network port is not the same as permission to check Windows. We need both a connection and the right target-scoped access.
bestPractices: Use a named account whose rights are limited to the intended member target.
Remove temporary target access when the agreed practice window ends.
commonMistakes: Domain Admin is far more access than this target needs. Don’t use it to skip the permissions lesson.
Keep SMB and RPC access limited to the scanner, not every address.
The browser uses 8834 to reach Nessus. The scanner uses different Windows protocols to check the target.

troubleshooting.problem: The target answers, but the account cannot sign in
troubleshooting.fix: Check the domain and username format, whether the account is enabled, the network-logon rules and the target’s Windows events.

troubleshooting.problem: Credentials pass, but local checks fail
troubleshooting.fix: Review the administrative shares, registry access and required WMI/RPC network paths with the target owner. Look for a relevant endpoint-policy event before changing anything.

lessons.pass: You have real credential-check saved result, or a clearly recorded failure, and an access plan limited to the intended member server.
lessons.exercise: Explain the difference between opening Nessus’s web page and letting Nessus check the Windows target. Show a redacted credential-check result for the latter.

quiz.question: Which account fits this member-server lab best?
options: A dedicated approved account scoped to this target
quiz.explanation: Grant only the access needed on the approved systems.

quiz.question: Does TCP 8834 replace SMB/WMI requirements?
quiz.explanation: 8834 serves the scanner’s HTTPS UI; target checks use their own protocols.

steps.title: Approve the Windows access route
steps.where: Windows Server 2022 member target · Computer Management and elevated PowerShell
actions: Use your separate Server 2022 member target, not a domain controller. For this route, we need a dedicated domain account that is an administrator only on this target—not Domain Admin. Finish the earlier Windows/AD and domain-join lessons first.

On the target, open Computer Management → Local Users and Groups → Groups → Administrators → Add. Under Locations, select the intended domain. Enter the dedicated scan username, click Check Names and confirm the exact identity before OK. Keep these rights limited to this target. If the account is missing, prepare it with the domain owner using the earlier Create Users & Policy lesson.

Work through the official Windows credentialed-scan things to prepare with the owner: rules for network sign-in, the administrative shares, Remote Registry and SMB/WMI access. These affect what Nessus can read inside Windows.
Using a standalone local account instead? Pause and follow Tenable’s separate local-account/UAC procedure with the owner. Don’t disable UAC everywhere or add an unreviewed registry workaround.

breakdown.meaning: Lists members of the local group so you can check the intended scan account without printing its password.
Identifies the built-in local Administrators group by its well-known ID, even when its displayed name is translated.
Reads the Remote Registry service status; it does not start it or change its startup policy.
Checks for the named administrative SMB shares on this target. Run elevated; do not create or expose shares blindly if policy disables them.

steps.expected: You have the intended target-scoped Windows account and a real record of the prerequisite checks.

steps.title: Review source-scoped firewall rules
steps.where: Windows Server 2022 target · Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security
actions: On the Windows target, click Start and open Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security. Under Inbound Rules, find the applicable File and Printer Sharing (SMB-In) and Windows Management Instrumentation rules.

For each rule the owner has agreed to use, right-click → Properties → Scope → Remote IP address → These IP addresses → Add. Enter the scanner’s exact address. On Advanced, select only the active permitted Private/Domain profile. Check the rule’s protocol and ports before enabling it. Windows checks may need SMB TCP445 and the documented WMI/RPC paths; TCP8834 is for the Nessus web page, not target login.

Review Remote Registry and the administrative shares with the owner. If a Remote Registry change is required and permitted, press Windows+R → services.msc → Remote Registry → Properties. Record the existing startup mode, apply only the agreed mode, and click Start. Note how you will restore the prior state after testing. Make one change at a time; leave firewall and endpoint protection enabled.
steps.expected: The needed Windows access rules and services are reviewed without exposing them to every source.

steps.title: Enter and test Windows credentials
steps.where: Your workstation browser · verified Nessus HTTPS console
actions: Edit the Windows target’s scan or policy. Open Credentials → Host → Windows, or Windows directly if that is how your version presents it. Enter the permitted account and secret in the real Nessus console, not in this learning page.
Use the actual domain field and username format that the chosen login method expects. A local account and a domain account are different identities. Save the job after checking the account.

Run Credential Validation if it is available, then read the host and plugin messages for login and local-check failures. Seeing a live target or open port445 is useful, but it doesn’t prove that Nessus successfully inspected Windows from inside.
steps.expected: The actual results tell you whether the account and local Windows checks worked, not just whether a port opened.

lessons.title: Protect Scan Credentials
lessons.description: Keep scan-account keys safe and plan when temporary access should end.
lessons.what: Passwords and private keys are like keys to a building. Let’s decide who holds them, where they stay, and when temporary keys should stop working.
lessons.why: A scanner may store access to several servers. Protecting that access matters just as much as protecting the reports it creates.
bestPractices: Use the approved password manager or secret store, and make temporary access short-lived when your lab supports that.
Treat scan reports as private information even after removing passwords. They may still describe weaknesses and server details.
commonMistakes: Check a screenshot before sharing it. A password or activation code visible in a corner is still exposed.
Don’t reuse your personal administrator password as a scan password across every target.

troubleshooting.problem: I shared a secret by mistake
troubleshooting.fix: Stop sharing the file and tell its owner. Revoke or rotate the exposed secret, then replace the saved result with a version that hides it.

lessons.pass: Your shared class notes contain no secrets, and someone is responsible for removing or rotating temporary access after the lab.
lessons.exercise: Look through the folder you intend to share. Remove or hide passwords, activation details and private keys before anyone else sees the evidence.

quiz.question: What belongs in your lab evidence?
options: A redacted status and account-owner reference
quiz.explanation: Saved result should prove the task without disclosing secrets.

quiz.question: When should temporary scan access be removed?
options: After the approved exercise or access window
Only if a scan finds nothing
quiz.explanation: Access should not outlive its approved purpose.

steps.title: Write a secret-handling plan
steps.where: Private lab notes · no scan launched
actions: Make a short account plan without writing down the password. Name the owner, why the account is needed, its permitted targets, the vault label, and when access should be rotated or removed.
Use different credentials for the Nessus control page and the target checks. Limit who can edit policies holding target credentials.
Before taking a screenshot, close or hide password fields, activation codes and private keys. Make sure you are using the scanner’s intended trusted HTTPS connection.
steps.expected: Your plan points to the protected secret store without copying the secrets.

Keep the relevant controls and computer context visible so you can explain the check. Hide credentials, activation details and private information first. This is your capture checklist; a genuine screenshot is still needed here.

steps.title: Review least privilege and cleanup
steps.where: Your workstation browser · verified Nessus HTTPS console
actions: Open each scan’s Credentials tab without revealing the stored values. Check that the account and sign-in method match your plan.
Ask the target owner to confirm that permissions cover only the agreed computers and checks. For SSH, use the least-privilege diagnostic saved result instead of simply allowing every command.
When the lab ends, remove temporary stored credentials from the scan jobs and revoke or rotate the temporary target access with its owner. Keep only saved result with secrets hidden.
steps.expected: Each stored account has a clear owner, purpose, target scope and cleanup date.

Keep the relevant controls and computer context visible so you can explain the check. Hide credentials, activation details and private information first. needs: Have the names of the account owners and your approved password-manager location. We need the plan, not the passwords themselves.

lessons.title: Add Only Authorized Targets
lessons.description: Double-check the target addresses against the computers in front of you.
lessons.what: We’ll compare each scan’s target field with the address shown on that target’s own console. This is a small check with a big payoff.
lessons.why: An old note or DNS record can point to the wrong computer. We don’t want last week’s address to decide what we check today.
bestPractices: Recheck target identities after automatic-address, DNS or network changes. Addresses can move even when your saved job stays the same.
commonMistakes: A /24 suffix describes a range, not one host. Keep our jobs to the exact permitted IPs.
Check today’s console address rather than trusting last week’s notes.

troubleshooting.problem: The name points to another computer
troubleshooting.fix: Pause the scan. Compare the DNS record with the target console and have the responsible owner correct the mismatch before continuing.

lessons.pass: Both exact target addresses match the current computers and the list you have permission to scan.
lessons.exercise: Read both target fields back to a partner or instructor. Compare them with the current console addresses and the agreed two-host list.

quiz.question: What does adding /24 usually do to an IPv4 target?
quiz.explanation: CIDR notation expands scope; it is not a single-host label.

quiz.question: What if the target IP no longer matches your record?
options: Scan the whole subnet to find it
quiz.explanation: Resolve the identity mismatch before sending scan traffic.

steps.title: Confirm each target at its console
steps.where: Alma and Windows target consoles
actions: On the Alma target, run hostname and ip -brief address. On Windows, run hostname and ipconfig. Write down what those computers show now, rather than copying an old note.
Compare both current addresses with the agreed list. They must be different from your scanner and your physical computer.
If a target’s address changed, update the permission record and any DNS entry as needed before editing the job. Don’t try an address just because it looks unused.
steps.command:
hostname
# AlmaLinux target only:
ip -brief address
# Windows target uses: ipconfig

breakdown.meaning: Prints the name of the current machine.
On AlmaLinux, shows a compact list of interface addresses; -brief changes the display, not networking.
On Windows, displays network adapter addressing. Run it in Windows, not in the Linux terminal.

steps.expected: Both target identities and current private addresses match the permitted list.

steps.title: Review both saved target fields
steps.where: Your workstation browser · verified Nessus HTTPS console
actions: Open the Alma scan’s Settings → Basic → Targets and compare the exact IP with your notes. Do the same for the Windows scan.
Leave off /24 and other CIDR suffixes; those can include a whole range. Don’t add a public website, router, scanner or domain controller to this class exercise.
Save, then ask a partner or instructor to read back the two permitted target addresses before you launch anything.
steps.expected: Both saved jobs contain exact checked target addresses, with no accidental subnet.

Keep the relevant controls and computer context visible so you can explain the check. Hide credentials, activation details and private information first. needs: Open both target consoles and your saved scan jobs. Don’t rely on an old screenshot or last week’s address list.

lessons.title: Run and Troubleshoot a Scan
lessons.description: Start one checked scan and stay with it while it runs.
lessons.what: Now we can launch an agreed job and watch what happens. We’ll check the target’s health, then read the results instead of relying only on a Completed label.
lessons.why: The job may finish while some checks failed. We need to know whether it reached the right host and successfully performed the checks we expected.
bestPractices: Watch both the target and scanner during the first run.
Keep the original starting point settings and saved result so a later comparison has a reliable starting point.
commonMistakes: Completed means the job ended. It does not guarantee every host and credentialed check succeeded.
If a job fails, investigate one copy. Launching many failed copies makes the problem harder to understand.

troubleshooting.problem: The scan remains pending
troubleshooting.fix: Check plugin preparation, current scanner load and the number of jobs your edition allows at once.

troubleshooting.problem: There are zero vulnerabilities
troubleshooting.fix: First check that the expected host was found and the intended authenticated checks worked. Fewer checks can produce fewer findings.

lessons.pass: You can show the intended target result and its coverage, or honestly explain why the attempt is still incomplete.
lessons.exercise: Choose one real warning or check result. Explain the smallest permitted diagnostic step that would help you understand it.

quiz.question: Does Completed mean every planned credentialed check succeeded?
quiz.explanation: Job status does not guarantee authentication or full coverage.

quiz.question: What should you do if the target becomes unstable?
options: Stop the scan and follow the agreed recovery plan
quiz.explanation: The target’s availability and the owner’s stop decision matter.

steps.title: Launch one approved job
steps.where: Your workstation browser · verified Nessus HTTPS console
actions: Before clicking Launch, read back the exact target, allowed time, account, policy revision and safe settings. Check that plugins are ready and that you know who to contact if the target has trouble.
Click Scans → My Scans. Find the intended job by name and click its launch/play icon. Start one target job, not several copies.
Stay nearby and watch the target’s health. If it becomes unstable or your stop contact asks you to stop, use the job’s stop control and follow the recovery plan you wrote down.
steps.expected: One intended job is running during the agreed window while you watch its health.

screenshot.title: Launch one approved job
screenshot.instructions: When you reach this point in your own lab, take a screenshot showing launch one approved job. Keep the relevant controls and computer context visible so you can explain the check. Hide credentials, activation details and private information first. This is your capture checklist; a genuine screenshot is still needed here.

steps.title: Read the completed host result
steps.where: Your workstation browser · verified Nessus HTTPS console
actions: When the job finishes, click it and open Hosts. Is the computer you expected actually there? Start with that simple check.
Open the host’s results and read Nessus Scan Information plus any authentication or permission findings. Check the scan time, plugin information and whether credentialed checks worked.
If a host is missing, credentials failed, plugins are stale or checks were blocked, record incomplete coverage. Fix the cause and rerun; don’t call the target safe because the job says Completed.
steps.expected: The target result includes an honest account of successful and incomplete checks.

screenshot.title: Read the completed host result
screenshot.instructions: When you reach this point in your own lab, take a screenshot showing read the completed host result. Keep the relevant controls and computer context visible so you can explain the check. Hide credentials, activation details and private information first. This is your capture checklist; a genuine screenshot is still needed here.

steps.title: Use a small troubleshooting ladder
steps.where: Scanner console and target console · approved diagnostics
actions: If no host appears, check that the target is on, then compare its real IP, route and VMware discovery setting. A computer can reject ping and still answer other traffic.

If login failed, compare the account format, password or key, permitted logon and SSH/SMB path. Read the target logs. If login worked but local checks failed, look at permissions and the services those checks need.

For a slow or failed job, check scanner load, storage, plugin preparation and simultaneous work. Try one permitted setting based on what you found. Don’t turn off firewalls or SELinux to make the symptom disappear.
steps.expected: You have a sensible next check based on the symptom, without switching security protections off.

needs: Finish the target, safe-settings and credential checks. Confirm the permitted scan time and who to contact if the target has trouble.

lessons.title: Read CVEs, CVSS and Plugin Evidence
lessons.description: Read one result carefully and explain the saved result behind its warning.
lessons.what: A finding is a warning with supporting details. A CVE names a publicly tracked vulnerability, while a plugin ID names Tenable’s check. They are different labels.
lessons.why: A severity color is a starting point, not the whole story. Reading the saved result helps us avoid mistaking an old-looking version or a missing permission for a proven problem.
bestPractices: Keep the actual plugin output and assessment time with your notes about a finding.
Ask the target owner to help check saved result that looks inconsistent with the installed system.
commonMistakes: A plugin ID identifies a Tenable check. It is not automatically a CVE number.
Technical severity helps with priority, but it does not tell us the whole business impact.
Don’t invent a dramatic result to finish the class. A real informational result or an honest no-finding note is better.

troubleshooting.problem: The finding seems wrong
troubleshooting.fix: Compare its plugin output with the real package or build and the vendor’s advisory. Keep the original result and write down how the owner resolved the question.

lessons.pass: You can explain a real finding without inventing a CVE or a score. If no applicable issue was observed, you can record that honestly too.
lessons.exercise: Write three sentences about a real result: what Nessus detected, what saved result supports it, and what you still need to check.

quiz.question: Must every informational finding have a CVE?
quiz.explanation: Information and configuration findings can exist without a CVE.

quiz.question: What should you read before choosing a fix?
options: Plugin output, affected target and solution
quiz.explanation: The actual saved result and vendor context guide the remediation.

steps.title: Open one finding
steps.where: Your workstation browser · verified Nessus HTTPS console
actions: Open a completed scan → Vulnerabilities. Pick one result that applies to your real target, then open it so we can read more than its color.
Read the plugin name and ID, description, affected host and port, suggested solution, and Plugin Output. Write down the actual detected product, version or setting behind the warning.
Record a CVE only when the result supplies one. Configuration and informational results may not have one, and that is normal.
steps.expected: Your note identifies the actual plugin, target and supporting saved result, with a CVE only if one is present.

screenshot.title: Open one finding
screenshot.instructions: When you reach this point in your own lab, take a screenshot showing open one finding. Keep the relevant controls and computer context visible so you can explain the check. Hide credentials, activation details and private information first. This is your capture checklist; a genuine screenshot is still needed here.

steps.title: Explain the score and its limits
steps.where: Your workstation browser · verified Nessus HTTPS console
actions: Look for the CVSS version, score and vector, if the finding has them. CVSS is a severity scoring system; its version and the assumptions shown in the vector help explain the number.

If the page also shows VPR, keep it separate from CVSS. CVSS describes technical severity. VPR uses Tenable’s changing threat-priority information. Neither number alone knows what this server means to your organization.

Check whether the warning relies on a version reported by the software. AlmaLinux may include a security fix without adopting the newest upstream version number; check the vendor advisory and package details before deciding. Record what still needs the owner’s review.
steps.expected: You can explain the score’s meaning and its limits using the real evidence.

screenshot.title: Explain the score and its limits
screenshot.instructions: When you reach this point in your own lab, take a screenshot showing explain the score and its limits. Keep the relevant controls and computer context visible so you can explain the check. Hide credentials, activation details and private information first. This is your capture checklist; a genuine screenshot is still needed here.

needs: Open a completed scan with its target and credential coverage checked. Keep the original result available while you read one finding.

lessons.title: Export a Useful Vulnerability Report
lessons.description: Turn useful scan details into a report the next person can understand.
lessons.what: We’ll prepare a handoff that tells a server owner what was checked, what was found and what needs attention. First, we’ll see which report formats your license allows.
lessons.why: A helpful report makes the next action clearer. It also explains what the scan could not check and keeps private information away from the wrong audience.
bestPractices: Open and read the report yourself before handing it to someone else.
Share only the detail the recipient needs for the agreed task.
commonMistakes: An older tutorial may describe different license features. Check what your own edition offers now.
A filter can hide hosts or findings. Review it before generating the report.

troubleshooting.problem: The PDF cannot be generated
troubleshooting.fix: Check the official things to prepare, including the supported Java/OpenJDK requirements where they apply. If needed, agree on another report format that your license permits.

lessons.pass: Your handoff clearly identifies its format, scope, date, coverage limits and private storage location.
lessons.exercise: Give your redacted report or clearly labeled manual worksheet to a partner. Ask them to find the target, saved result and suggested next action.

quiz.question: Can current Nessus Essentials export reports according to the 10.12 guide?
quiz.explanation: The current guide explicitly limits exports/reports; check your edition.

quiz.question: Can report filters change what appears in a report?
options: Only if the firewall is off
quiz.explanation: Check the visible results and selections before generating the report.

steps.title: Check the report entitlement
steps.where: Your workstation browser · verified Nessus HTTPS console
actions: Open Settings → About and check your actual edition. In the 10.12 guide, Essentials cannot create scan exports or reports, while Essentials Plus offers PDF and HTML reports. Let’s use what your license really provides.
If your edition lacks the export you need, write that down and make a manual worksheet with private details hidden. Label it as your worksheet, not a Nessus export.
For a licensed report, open the completed scan and check active filters and selected Hosts or Vulnerabilities. They change what the generated report includes.
steps.expected: You know whether to use a licensed export or a clearly labeled manual worksheet.

screenshot.title: Check the report entitlement

Keep the relevant controls and computer context visible so you can explain the check. Hide credentials, activation details and private information first. steps.title: Generate and inspect the report
steps.where: Your workstation browser · verified Nessus HTTPS console
actions: If reports are included, open the completed scan and click Report. Choose an available format and template; for CSV, select the columns you need. Then click Generate Report.
Open the downloaded file privately. Check the target, date, plugin IDs, severity, saved result and solution. Include the scanner/plugin date and any login or coverage limits in your handoff notes.

Save the results in the agreed private saved result folder. Keep reports, target lists, licenses and secrets out of GitHub. If your license lacks CSV or PDF, use a permitted alternative or your clearly labeled worksheet.
steps.expected: The checked report or worksheet is stored privately and explains what was and was not covered.

screenshot.title: Generate and inspect the report

Keep the relevant controls and computer context visible so you can explain the check. Hide credentials, activation details and private information first. needs: Have a completed scan with checked coverage. Know your Nessus edition and the private folder where you may store results.

lessons.title: Prioritize and Fix One Finding
lessons.description: Choose a real issue to fix and make a plan before changing the server.
lessons.what: Remediation means fixing the cause of a finding. Let’s choose one real issue, agree on a supported remedy and protect a way back before we touch the target.
lessons.why: The highest score is not always the first job. Exposure, business importance and saved result help the owner decide what needs attention first.
bestPractices: Make one planned change at a time and keep a way to recover.
Use the vendor’s advisory to identify the actual fixed package or build, not a guessed version.
commonMistakes: Hiding a finding or lowering its severity does not fix the underlying problem.
Read the computer name before changing it, even if a console is already open.

troubleshooting.problem: The application fails after the change
troubleshooting.fix: Stop and keep the relevant logs. Tell the owner and follow the agreed recovery branch. Don’t stack several unrelated changes on top of the first problem.

lessons.pass: The owner has agreed to the chosen fix, and your notes show the change that actually happened. We still need a rescan before calling the issue verified fixed.
lessons.exercise: Explain why you chose this issue first. Include the saved result, the server’s purpose and the approved recovery plan.

quiz.question: Which action is real remediation?
options: Applying the approved fix to the affected target
quiz.explanation: Remediation changes the cause of the finding, not its visibility.

quiz.question: What if no suitable real finding exists?
options: Record the result and request an approved exercise
quiz.explanation: An honest result is better than fabricated saved result or unnecessary exposure.

steps.title: Choose and plan a real fix
steps.where: Private finding worksheet · target owner review
actions: Choose one real finding that has a supported fix from the vendor. Write down the plugin or CVE if present, the affected target, saved result, owner, proposed change and due date.

Talk through why this issue comes first: who can reach it, saved result of exploitation, how important the server is and which protections already exist. The biggest color or score is not the only reason.

Write down the backup, rebuild or rollback path, the permitted maintenance time and your application checks. If there is no suitable real finding, tell the instructor and ask for an approved exercise. Don’t weaken a system or invent a vulnerability.
steps.expected: The selected fix has an agreed owner, reason, change window and recovery plan.

screenshot.title: Choose and plan a real fix
screenshot.instructions: When you reach this point in your own lab, take a screenshot showing choose and plan a real fix. Keep the relevant controls and computer context visible so you can explain the check. Hide credentials, activation details and private information first. This is your capture checklist; a genuine screenshot is still needed here.

steps.title: Apply the approved vendor remedy
steps.where: Only the affected target console · approved maintenance window
actions: Before making the change, read the target name again. Follow the vendor’s exact fix and the change plan agreed with the person responsible for this server.

For AlmaLinux, identify the actual affected package from the plugin and vendor advisory before choosing an update. For Windows, follow the required supported update or settings procedure. Restart only at the agreed time.

Keep the command or clicks you really used, the result and the application-health checks. Hiding a plugin or lowering its severity is not a fix. We still need to rescan before saying the issue is gone.
steps.expected: The real change and application-health result are recorded. Verification still waits for the rescan.

screenshot.title: Apply the approved vendor remedy
screenshot.instructions: When you reach this point in your own lab, take a screenshot showing apply the approved vendor remedy. Keep the relevant controls and computer context visible so you can explain the check. Hide credentials, activation details and private information first. This is your capture checklist; a genuine screenshot is still needed here.

needs: Choose a real finding with a vendor-supported remedy. Have the owner’s permission, a change window and a recovery plan before starting.

lessons.title: Rescan and Prove the Fix
lessons.description: Check the same target again and see whether the fix really worked.
lessons.what: We’ll ask Nessus to check the affected computer again using equivalent coverage. Then we’ll compare the saved result before and after the change.
lessons.why: A warning disappearing only helps if the new scan actually checked the same thing. Failed credentials can make results look better while giving us less information.
bestPractices: Keep both sets of saved result and record changes to the policy, plugin date or access.
commonMistakes: Fewer findings from a scan that could not sign in are not proof of a fix.
Compare the same target and equivalent settings, not two different hosts or templates.

troubleshooting.problem: The original finding is still present
troubleshooting.fix: Confirm that you changed the intended host, completed any needed restart and installed the supported package, build or setting from the vendor remedy.

lessons.pass: You can explain why the saved result supports a fix, why the issue remains, or why there is not enough saved result to decide yet.
lessons.exercise: Write a short before-and-after explanation. Use your real results and explain any difference in settings, plugins or access.

quiz.question: The finding disappeared, but SSH authentication failed. What is the result?
quiz.explanation: Missing local-check coverage cannot prove a local vulnerability was fixed.

quiz.question: Should you keep the original baseline?
quiz.explanation: It shows what was observed before the change and supports comparison.

steps.title: Run the verification job
steps.where: Your workstation browser · verified Nessus HTTPS console
actions: Check that the verification job uses the same target, equivalent policy and port coverage, working credentials and ready plugins. Note any plugin date or setting changes that affect the comparison.
Launch the verification job during the permitted time. Keep the original scan and report so you can compare them; don’t delete the baseline.
When it finishes, confirm the host identity, credentialed-check success and relevant plugin saved result before comparing the warning.
steps.expected: The verification scan completes with the required target identity and useful coverage checked.

screenshot.title: Run the verification job
screenshot.instructions: When you reach this point in your own lab, take a screenshot showing run the verification job. Keep the relevant controls and computer context visible so you can explain the check. Hide credentials, activation details and private information first. This is your capture checklist; a genuine screenshot is still needed here.

steps.title: Record the verification decision
steps.where: Nessus results and private remediation worksheet
actions: Compare the same host and plugin in the old and new results. Also check the real installed package, build or setting against the vendor’s fix.

If the warning disappears but login failed or coverage changed, record “inconclusive”—we don’t yet know. If it remains, review the saved result, any required reboot and patch applicability with the owner.
Close the item only when the saved result is good enough and the owner agrees. Record the fix date, verification date, rescan ID and any remaining risk.
steps.expected: Your decision is supported by saved result: fixed, still present, or not enough information yet.

screenshot.title: Record the verification decision
screenshot.instructions: When you reach this point in your own lab, take a screenshot showing record the verification decision. Keep the relevant controls and computer context visible so you can explain the check. Hide credentials, activation details and private information first. This is your capture checklist; a genuine screenshot is still needed here.

needs: Keep the original scan and change record. Make sure the same target, required credentials and equivalent scan settings are ready.

lessons.title: Schedule Scans and Watch Scanner Health
lessons.description: Plan the next scan and learn a few checks that keep the scanner healthy.
lessons.what: Let’s put permitted scans on a calendar, if your edition supports that, and check whether the scanner has enough room and resources to do the work.
lessons.why: A calendar entry does not guarantee a good scan. Full disks, stale plugins, sleeping targets and overlapping jobs can all get in the way.
bestPractices: Write the time zone along with the permitted maintenance time.
Read failed or skipped job results. A calendar entry cannot guarantee that a useful scan actually happened.
commonMistakes: Turn off recurring practice scans when the class ends. Don’t leave unattended jobs behind.
More simultaneous jobs won’t help a scanner that is already overloaded.

troubleshooting.problem: A scheduled job did not run
troubleshooting.fix: Check the service, schedule, time zone, license, plugin readiness and other running jobs. Find the cause before creating duplicate schedules.

lessons.pass: You can explain the next agreed scan time and show how you would notice a scanner or job that needs attention.
lessons.exercise: Write a five-item weekly scanner checklist. Include a stop date for practice schedules so they don’t keep running after the lab ends.

quiz.question: What must a schedule include to avoid time confusion?
options: A declared time zone and approved window
quiz.explanation: The displayed time must be interpreted in the intended time zone.

quiz.question: What should happen to a practice schedule after the lab?
options: Disable it or transfer it to an approved owner
quiz.explanation: Scanning must not continue beyond the agreed scope and ownership.

steps.title: Set an approved schedule
steps.where: Your workstation browser · verified Nessus HTTPS console
actions: Agree on a time when scanning is allowed and the targets will be on. Open the saved scan → Settings → Basic → Schedule.
If your edition offers scheduling, enable it, choose the agreed frequency, date, time and time zone, then Save. SONIC-Academy does not create that schedule for you.

Read back the next run time and check for overlapping jobs. If scheduling is unavailable, use a clearly recorded manual checklist or calendar reminder instead. Disable practice schedules when you finish the lab.
steps.expected: You can read back the next run time and time zone, or your documented manual alternative.

steps.title: Inspect scanner health and updates
steps.where: Your workstation browser · verified Nessus HTTPS console
actions: If your edition and role provide it, open Settings → Scanner Health. Look through Overview, Network and Alerts for signs that the scanner is short of resources or busy with other scans.
Open Settings → About and review plugin readiness and update status. Compare a slow job with real load, free disk space and other running jobs before changing performance settings.
Make a routine checklist: service running, enough storage, healthy updates, correct targets, successful credentialed checks, completed jobs and protected report storage.
steps.expected: You can point to the health checks that help you spot a scanner needing attention.

needs: Have a saved scan, an agreed maintenance time and the correct time zone. Scheduling is optional if your license does not provide it.

lessons.title: Connect Findings to ACAS, STIGs, RMF and POA&Ms
lessons.description: See where scan results fit into bigger company and government security work.
lessons.what: Nessus checks systems; Tenable Security Center is a separate management platform. ACAS-style work adds rules about who may scan, who reviews results and who tracks the fixes.
lessons.why: A scan report can help someone make a decision, but it cannot approve a system for use or prove that every security rule has been checked.
bestPractices: Keep vulnerability findings, compliance checks and risk decisions separate in your explanation.
For real work, use the current requirements and approval process that actually apply to the organization.
commonMistakes: Nessus and Security Center are separate products, even when an organization uses them together.
No CVEs found does not mean every STIG configuration requirement passed.
Different organizations have different required deadlines. Don’t invent one universal deadline for every finding.

troubleshooting.problem: The scan report and compliance checklist disagree
troubleshooting.fix: Review which systems and checks were included, account permissions, the audit version and the applicable requirements with the assessor. Keep both kinds of saved result while resolving the difference.

lessons.pass: You can explain what your scan saved result supports and what still needs a separate compliance, risk or authorization decision.
lessons.exercise: Make one clearly labeled training POA&M-style row. Explain who would own the fix and which real role would decide whether remaining risk can be accepted.

quiz.question: Does a clean vulnerability scan prove STIG compliance?
quiz.explanation: Configuration audits and manual requirements are separate evidence.

quiz.question: Who grants risk acceptance or an authorization decision?
options: The designated authority under the organization’s process
quiz.explanation: The tool informs a decision; it does not replace accountable approval.

steps.title: Separate the products and evidence types
steps.where: Private lab notes · no scan launched
actions: Let’s separate three names in your notes: Nessus is the scanner; Security Center is a separate management and analysis platform; ACAS is a DoD program context, not the name of this standalone license.
Explain two different questions: a vulnerability scan asks about weaknesses; a compliance audit checks particular configuration requirements. No vulnerability findings does not prove STIG compliance.

For a permitted licensed compliance exercise, choose the current audit that applies to the exact OS and version, using Tenable and DISA guidance. Essentials and Essentials Plus do not include compliance templates. A RHEL STIG does not automatically apply to AlmaLinux; the responsible authority must decide applicability.
steps.expected: You can distinguish vulnerability saved result, compliance saved result and the separate decision to accept risk.

steps.title: Create a practice POA&M-style record
steps.where: Private lab notes · no scan launched
actions: Make one practice record for a reviewed real finding. Include the asset, plugin or CVE when it has one, what is wrong, saved result date, why it matters, who owns the fix, milestones, due date and how you plan to check the fix.
Label the row a training worksheet, not an official agency POA&M. Real organizations set their own required format, deadlines and approval process.

Think of RMF as the wider risk-management process. Scan saved result can help assessment and continuing monitoring, but designated officials decide risk acceptance and authorization. A clean scan or changed color does not grant an authorization to operate.
steps.expected: Your training worksheet clearly names ownership and follow-up without pretending to be an official agency approval.

lessons.title: Final Lab: Scan, Fix and Verify Two Targets
lessons.description: Put the whole process together: scan two targets, explain a result, fix one issue and check again.
lessons.what: This is your chance to lead the work. We’ll start with permission and target identity, run the agreed checks, review real saved result, make one supported fix and verify it.
lessons.why: A careful, explainable process is more useful than a dramatic result. Someone else should be able to see how you reached your conclusion.
bestPractices: Ask your instructor to review the final saved result pack with you.
Keep detailed reports, passwords, license files and private keys out of the repository.
commonMistakes: A simulated picture or capture reminder is not a real scan result.
Call a fix verified only after an equivalent, successful rescan and the relevant saved result checks.

troubleshooting.problem: A required part of the lab is unavailable
troubleshooting.fix: Keep the practical marked unfinished. Save the plan and the saved result you really collected, then resume when the permitted systems, files or license are available.

lessons.pass: Your instructor can follow permission → target identity → useful scan coverage → finding → approved fix → valid rescan → cleanup. If real scanning or fixing was not possible, the practical remains unfinished.
lessons.exercise: Present your redacted saved result pack and explain one limitation or remaining question out loud. Let your instructor trace the work from permission through cleanup.

quiz.question: How many machines does the final lab require?
options: Three: scanner plus two separate targets
quiz.explanation: Nessus self-scanning is unsupported for this vulnerability exercise.

quiz.question: When can the final practical be called verified?
options: When real authorized scan/change/rescan evidence passes review
quiz.explanation: Learning-page progress is not proof that a real-world scan or remediation succeeded.

steps.title: Approve and inspect the two-target plan
steps.where: Private lab notes · no scan launched
actions: Bring up three separate consoles: the scanner, AlmaLinux 9 target and Windows Server 2022 member target. Read back their identities and the exact two target IPs. The scanner is not one of the vulnerability targets.
Check the scope agreement, private network, license, account owner, safe settings, recovery plan, scan time and stop contact. Leave the scanner and all unrelated devices out of the target fields.

Make two named saved jobs, one for each target. Where your license supports it, use the reviewed starting point policy for both. Add the right permitted SSH or Windows credentials and finish the credential checks.
steps.expected: Your two saved target jobs match the reviewed private-lab plan and have checked credentials.

steps.title: Run and explain the actual baseline
steps.where: Your workstation browser · verified Nessus HTTPS console
actions: Launch the Alma job first and watch it. Check the expected host and credentialed-check coverage when it finishes. Run the Windows job when your resources and license allow it.
For each target, record the actual date, plugin set, coverage and one meaningful result. An informational result is fine; never invent a vulnerability or a target finding count.

With your instructor, select a real finding and explain its plugin saved result, CVE/CVSS information when present, exposure and fix priority. Make the licensed report or a clearly labeled manual worksheet.
steps.expected: You have two real target assessments with honest coverage notes and no invented findings.

steps.title: Remediate one issue and prove the result
steps.where: Affected target console, then Nessus results
actions: With the owner’s agreement, apply one supported fix to a real issue and record the application and recovery checks. If there is no suitable issue, explain that to the instructor instead of weakening the target to make one appear.

Rescan the affected target with equivalent coverage and working credentials. Compare the real before-and-after evidence. Mark the issue fixed, still present or inconclusive according to what the checks support.
Present the scope note, redacted scan saved result, change worksheet and verification decision. Remove temporary access and turn off practice schedules when the exercise ends.
steps.expected: Your saved result pack shows the fix and valid rescan, or clearly explains which real-world checks remain unfinished.

needs: Have one ready scanner, two separate ready targets, agreed scope, working scan accounts and a recovery plan. Finish the earlier checks before this final run.

supplies: A working Nessus 10.12.5 scanner from either installation class, with its plugins ready and its real license checked.
Two separate practice target VMs: AlmaLinux 9 and Windows Server 2022. Keep both separate from the Nessus scanner.
The private VMware lab network and a note with all three computers’ actual private addresses. We will scan only the two targets.
Permission to scan those exact target addresses during an agreed practice time, plus a person to contact if something stops working.
Dedicated target login accounts with the permissions needed for your checks. For the Windows domain-account route, prepare DC01 and domain membership first.
A private notes folder for results, a recovery plan for the targets and enough resources to run the scanner and the targets without exhausting your host.
